description: We are a passionate team interested in space, science, and technology. We aim to solve real-world challenges through innovation and teamwork. Looking for enthusiastic members skilled in coding, AI/ML, research, and creative problem-solving.
summary: Homeward is a Martian map, built only from real data, that plans a walk on Mars and always gets the walker home. On Mars, help is about 11 light-minutes away, so a crew member walking out from the habitat must know at every step how long the walk home takes, and whether air, power, radiation dose and daylight will last. That data already exists across many NASA missions, but no map brings it together for one walk. Homeward fuses nine kinds of data from seven missions into one 3D map: MOLA and HRSC relief, HiRISE, CTX, THEMIS, geology, thermal inertia, weather, radiation and space weather. It plans a route that avoids slopes and rocks a suit cannot cross, keeps every budget with a walk-back reserve, and guides the walk with a live helmet display that includes radio line of sight to the habitat. Every number is measured, computed or cited. It is free and runs in any browser.
details:
What it does. Homeward turns NASA’s Mars data into one map a crew can trust for a Marswalk. It runs one loop: Explore, Brief, Plan, Walk, Home.

  • Explore: a Google-Earth style 3D globe with real 200 m relief everywhere (MOLA and Mars Express HRSC) and 1 m HiRISE terrain at Gale Crater.
    • Search 2,064 named places and tour 13 landing sites, from Mars 3 to Zhurong.
    • See Spirit’s and Opportunity’s drive paths and the Viking 1 and 2 landing-site mosaics from JPL Mars Trek.
    • Turn on overlays for geology, thermal inertia and dust.
    • Any spot shows its USGS rock unit and every published USGS geologic map that covers it.
    • HiRISE stereo terrain becomes a 2 m slope and rock grid; cells steeper than 20° or with more than 1 m of rock relief are blocked.
    • An A* search finds the fastest route, using Tobler’s hiking function scaled to the Apollo walk-back rate of 3.3 km/h.
    • A Dijkstra “walk-back field” gives the time home from every point, so the plan checks the way home at every step, not just at the turnaround.
    • Life support (8 h minus a 30 min reserve), daylight, dose and the 2 km radius are hard budgets; any breach blocks approval.
  • Walk: walk it yourself at the planner’s pace, follow the plan, or fly anywhere at 10 to 1,000 m/s. The helmet display shows time home, air, dose, daylight and radio line of sight to the habitat, computed over the real terrain and the planet’s curvature.
  • Rover view: street view from Curiosity’s and Perseverance’s own photos, each placed where its camera pointed, plus the newest raw images from Mars.
  • Suit assistant: answers by voice, only with numbers the app computes, and names its sources.

Worked example. On sol 182 the walk from the habitat to the rock where Curiosity found an ancient lake is 905 m and 17 minutes of walking. It uses 1 h 17 min of the 7 h 30 min life-support budget, keeps at least a 6 h 13 min walk-back margin, and costs 0.034 mSv. The verdict is GO.

Benefits and impact.

  • Crew safety: the time home is known at every step.
  • Mission planning: orbiter and rover data are fused into one view.
  • Education: anyone can walk Mars for free.

Tools.

  • Code: TypeScript, React 19 and Vite; CesiumJS for 3D; Web Workers for terrain decoding and planning; zod validation.
  • On-device voice: Kokoro-82M and Whisper.
  • Server and data: Vercel serverless functions, and a Python data pipeline (NumPy, rasterio).
  • Testing: 84 automated tests, checked against published values from Mars24, NASA and ESA light times, and JPL Horizons.
  • Hosting: free, on Vercel’s Hobby plan.

What is creative. It is the first map to plan a Mars walk with the way home guaranteed at every step. Rover street view is built from NASA’s raw photos and camera models. Every number on screen carries a badge (MEASURED, COMPUTED, STANDARD or ASSUMPTION) and a source.

Factors we considered. Astronaut safety first; honest data (no demo numbers, and weather always dated); offline use; zero cost; a strict security policy; and screens from a habitat display to a tablet or a helmet HUD.
